sound_highlight: [ẽj̃]  nasal “ayn,” not a consonant m
note: 3rd person of ter (você / ele / ela tem). The ending -em is a nasal diphthong.

sound_highlight: [ɲ]  palatal “ny”; the n is not a separate [n]
note: 1st person of ter (eu tenho). The vowel before nh is nasal. Final -o is [u].

sound_highlight: [ẽ]  nasal vowel, no n consonant | [dʒi]  “jee” (d palatalizes before this [i])
note: 3rd person of entender. Unstressed final e sounds like [i], so de becomes [dʒi] in Rio and São Paulo.

sound_highlight: [ɛ]  open “eh,” and the accent marks it
note: Form of ser: “is / you are.”

sound_highlight: [i]  “ee,” no accent
note: The conjunction “and”: você e eu.

sound_highlight: [ej]  diphthong, like English “say”
note: 1st person of saber (eu sei). Irregular: not *sabo.

sound_highlight: [i]  unstressed final e is “ee”
note: 3rd person of saber (você / ele / ela sabe). The b stays [b].

sound_highlight: [ũj]  nasal diphthong, even with no tilde
note: Adverb / adjective “very; a lot.” A well-known spelling quirk.

sound_highlight: [ɐ̃w̃]  nasal “own”; the tilde marks it
note: “No / not.”

sound_highlight: [u]  plain “oo,” no tilde — this is em + o
note: Contraction of em + o (“in the, at the”). Not a nasal.

sound_highlight: [u]  unstressed article, sounds like “oo”
note: The masculine singular article “the.”

sound_highlight: [ɔ]  open “aw,” marked by the accent
note: The noun “dollar.” The accent marks both stress and the open vowel.

sound_highlight: [zi]  the irregular -ze, from Latin -decim
note: 11. First of the -ze teens (Latin ūndecim, one + ten).

sound_highlight: [zi]  same -ze as onze–quinze
note: 12. Latin duodecim, two + ten. Also the root of dúzia (dozen).

sound_highlight: [zi]  same -ze family
note: 13. Latin tredecim, three + ten.

sound_highlight: [zi]  last consonant of the -ze teens, with catorze / quatorze
note: 14. Also spelled quatorze. Latin quattuordecim.

sound_highlight: [zi]  last of the irregular -ze forms
note: 15. After this, 16–19 switch to dez + e + the unit.

sound_highlight: dez  ‘ten’ | seis  ‘six’ — the whole word is dez e seis
note: 16. The transparent pattern begins: dezesseis = dez e seis.

sound_highlight: dez  ‘ten’ | sete  ‘seven’
note: 17. dez e sete, written as one word.

sound_highlight: dez  ‘ten’ | oito  ‘eight’ — the e is swallowed in the spelling
note: 18. dez e oito → dezoito.

sound_highlight: dez  ‘ten’ | nove  ‘nine’
note: 19. Last of the ‘ten-and-’ teens.

sound_highlight: [ˈvĩtʃi]  a new root, from Latin vīgintī — not *dez e dez
note: 20. After this, 21 is vinte e um, on the same model as cento e um.

sound_highlight: [ẽj̃]  nasal diphthong, the same ending as in tem — used standing alone
note: 100 on its own: cem reais. Before another number, use cento.

sound_highlight: [ẽ]  nasal vowel (no n consonant), then [tu] — the combining form
note: Used in 101+: cento e um, cento e vinte.

sound_highlight: [s]  no t — ‘that’ (near the listener); also the casual all-purpose form
note: Demonstrative. In everyday Brazilian speech, isso often covers ‘this’ and ‘that.’

sound_highlight: [st]  the t is the whole difference — ‘this’ near the speaker
note: Demonstrative. More precise when the thing is right here, in the speaker’s hands.

sound_highlight: [ki]  a plain “kee,” no nasal
note: ‘What.’ In questions about a thing, it usually comes as o que.

sound_highlight: [ẽj̃]  nasal diphthong, the same ending as in tem — not a consonant m
note: ‘Who.’ Quem é? is the usual ‘Who is it?’
